--- title: "A million points on the GPU" description: "One million points of a Clifford attractor that pan and zoom at full frame rate. Past 50,000 records, as_widget() redraws the zoomed view with WebGL2 instead of a 2D canvas." categories: [Interactive, Big data] image: figs/webgl-million.png --- A [big scatter](big-interactive.qmd) stays interactive because `as_widget()` ships one embedded image plus a compact index in place of a node per point. Zooming redraws the visible points on top of that image so they stay sharp. On a 2D canvas that redraw costs about a second per frame at a million points, which makes panning feel stuck. From 50,000 records up, the widget does the redraw with WebGL2. Every point is one instance of a small quad, and a fragment shader cuts out the marker shape, so the GPU draws the whole list in a single call. On a laptop a zoom frame over a million points takes about 30 ms on the GPU, against roughly 1.3 s on the canvas. The data is one orbit of a Clifford attractor: each point comes from the one before it. Colour shows how far the orbit jumped to get there, split into five equal-count bands. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} n <- 1e6 a <- -1.4; b <- 1.6; c <- 1.0; d <- 0.7 x <- y <- numeric(n) x0 <- y0 <- 0.1 for (i in seq_len(n)) { x1 <- sin(a * y0) + c * cos(a * x0) y1 <- sin(b * x0) + d * cos(b * y0) x[i] <- x1; y[i] <- y1 x0 <- x1; y0 <- y1 } step <- c(0, sqrt(diff(x)^2 + diff(y)^2)) speed <- cut( step, quantile(step, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE, labels = c("slowest", "slow", "middle", "fast", "fastest") ) df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, speed = speed, id = seq_len(n)) pal <- c( slowest = "#f6d186", slow = "#f19b5c", middle = "#d9534f", fast = "#8e3b88", fastest = "#3d5a98" ) ink <- "#d8cfbd" p <- vplot(df, width = 8, height = 7) |> mark_point( x = x, y = y, color = speed, data_id = id, tooltip = speed, size = 0.12, alpha = 0.3 ) |> scale_color_manual(values = pal) |> guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 3))) |> coord_fixed() |> labs(title = "A million points of a Clifford attractor", color = "step length") |> theme_void() |> theme( plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#14110f", color = NA), plot.margin = c(5.5, 5.5, 5.5, 5.5), plot.title = element_text(color = "#f4eee0", size = 16), legend.title = element_text(color = ink), legend.text = element_text(color = ink) ) ``` ::: Hover a point for its band and scroll to zoom into one of the folds. Dragging brushes a selection; to pan instead, click the drag-mode button at the left of the toolbar until it shows the hand, or use the arrow keys. `legend_click = "hide"` turns the legend into a filter: click a swatch to hide its band, double-click to show that band on its own, and double-click it again to bring the others back. The GPU redraws the million points each time, with no image rebuilt. The whole page is about 8 MB: the full view ships as one image, and the index stores each point in a few bytes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as_widget(p, height = 630, legend_click = "hide") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Choosing the renderer `render_options(webgl = "auto")` is the default. It uses WebGL2 for any draw list of 50,000 records or more and keeps the 2D canvas below that, where the canvas is already fast. `webgl = "always"` uses the GPU for every list and `webgl = "never"` turns it off: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as_widget(p, render = render_options(webgl = "never")) ``` ::: If the browser has no WebGL2 context, or a list holds something the GPU path does not draw (gradients, dashed strokes, grouped marks, very large paths), that list falls back to the canvas on its own. The points look the same either way, so `"auto"` is safe to leave on.
